etymology: From the leather stock, a stiff collar of black leather, worn by American and British Marines (and soldiers). The USMC History Division’s Marine Corps Lore (Historical Reference Series No. 22, 1960) records that from 1798 “one stock of black leather and clasp” was issued to each U.S. Marine every year. The collar stood nearly three and a half inches high and buckled at the back. It survived the uniform changes of 1833, 1839 and 1859 and was dropped in 1872. The National Museum of the Marine Corps, citing J. E. Lighter’s Historical Dictionary of American Slang, dates the earliest unequivocal printed use of leatherneck to 1889–90, applied to the Royal Marines; American use follows by the end of the nineteenth century. A minority account, told by H. L. Mencken and William Morris, holds that British sailors meant the Marines’ unwashed necks, not their collars.
biblical_def: Leatherneck is the oldest of the Marine nicknames, and the History Division counts it as tradition rather than legend: three generations of Marines wore the leather stock, so the name needs no theory. The collar was meant for full dress. The History Division notes that it could hardly be worn in battle because it stopped the neck from turning to sight along a barrel, and that it was supposed to improve bearing by forcing the chin up; General George F. Elliott, remembering it after the Civil War, said it made the wearers look “like geese looking for rain.” The Christian observation: Scripture speaks often of the neck. A neck held stiff against God is rebellion, “Ye stiffnecked and uncircumcised in heart and ears, ye do always resist the Holy Ghost” (Act 7:51). The godly man wears another collar: “Let not mercy and truth forsake thee: bind them about thy neck” (Pro 3:3). A Marine’s bearing is a good thing; a proud neck before God is not.
webster_summary: A U.S. Marine; from the stiff leather stock issued to Marines from 1798 until 1872 (USMC History Division). Scripture prizes mercy and truth bound about the neck, not a neck stiffened against God (Pro 3:3; Act 7:51).
webster_full: LEATHERNECK, n. (Marine Corps) A U.S. Marine. From the black leather stock, or high collar, issued to Marines from 1798 and dropped from the uniform in 1872 (USMC History Division, Marine Corps Lore, 1960).
scriptures: Let not mercy and truth forsake thee: bind them about thy neck; write them upon the table of thine heart:
Ye stiffnecked and uncircumcised in heart and ears, ye do always resist the Holy Ghost: as your fathers did, so do ye.
Because I knew that thou art obstinate, and thy neck is an iron sinew, and thy brow brass;
corruption_summary: An honourable nickname with a plain origin; the only danger is mistaking a stiff collar for a stiff neck before God.
corruption_paragraphs: The leather stock was issued to hold a Marine’s head up, and good bearing is no sin. The danger is the old one of mistaking outward stiffness for inward strength. Israel was called stiffnecked not because it stood straight but because it would not bow (Isa 48:4).
The Marine who knows his Bible keeps both: a straight back before men and a bowed neck before God, with mercy and truth bound about it (Pro 3:3).
roots_summary: leather + neck → the black leather stock issued to U.S. Marines from 1798 → dropped from the uniform in 1872 → nickname for a Marine (USMC History Division).
roots_lines: 1798: “one stock of black leather and clasp” issued yearly to each U.S. Marine (USMC History Division)
Stock survives the uniform changes of 1833, 1839 and 1859
1872: stock dropped from the Marine uniform
1889–90: earliest unequivocal printed use of leatherneck, for the Royal Marines (NMMC, citing Lighter)
End of the 1800s: American use as a name for U.S. Marines (NMMC)
usage: “Grandpa was a leatherneck at Inchon, and he still stands like one.”
Let not mercy and truth forsake thee: bind them about thy neck (Pro 3:3).

etymology: Said to translate German Teufelhunden. The USMC History Division’s Marine Corps Lore (1960) gives the traditional story: German troops at Belleau Wood in June 1918 called the Marines Teufelhunden. Later History Division scholarship contradicts the date. Writing in Marine Corps History (Marine Corps University Press, Winter 2022), James P. Gregory finds that no evidence shows the name came from the Germans; it was in American newspapers by April 1918, while the 4th Brigade was in the Toulon sector near Verdun and before Belleau Wood, and the Marine’s letter that the 13 April article cited has never been found. The National Museum of the Marine Corps points to a Boston Daily Globe story of 14 April 1918 (“Recruiters Report a New Nickname for Marines”) and notes that correct German would be Teufelshunde. Who first coined it is unknown; the Belleau Wood version does not fit the dates.
biblical_def: Devil dog is the Marine Corps’ most loved nickname, and its usual origin story is wrong in its details. The tradition says the Germans gave the name after Belleau Wood. The record shows the name was already in American papers in April 1918, weeks before that battle, credited to the Germans by recruiters and by a letter no one has produced. The History Division’s own journal says so plainly, and says that the Corps wore the name as a badge of honour anyway. The Christian observation: a good name does not need a false story to hold it up. “Thou shalt not raise a false report” (Exo 23:1). The Marines of 1918 earned their reputation in the Toulon sector and at Belleau Wood whatever any German called them, and the truth honours them better than the legend: “A faithful witness will not lie” (Pro 14:5).
webster_summary: A U.S. Marine; traditionally from German Teufelhunden at Belleau Wood (June 1918), but the name was in American newspapers by April 1918 and no German source has been found (USMC History Division; NMMC). Origin disputed.
webster_full: DEVIL DOG, n. (Marine Corps) A U.S. Marine. Traditionally said to render German Teufelhunden, a name the Germans supposedly gave Marines at Belleau Wood in 1918; the name appears in American newspapers by April 1918, before that battle, and no German use has been documented (Marine Corps History Division; National Museum of the Marine Corps).
scriptures: Thou shalt not raise a false report: put not thine hand with the wicked to be an unrighteous witness.
A faithful witness will not lie: but a false witness will utter lies.

Finally, brethren, whatsoever things are true, whatsoever things are honest, whatsoever things are just, whatsoever things are pure, whatsoever things are lovely, whatsoever things are of good report; if there be any virtue, and if there be any praise, think on these things.
corruption_summary: A proud nickname wrapped in a story the record does not support; honour the Marines with the true history, not the recruiting legend.
corruption_paragraphs: The Teufelhunden story made a fine recruiting poster, and the Corps used it for decades. The problem is not the nickname but the habit of repeating a story because it flatters us. A legend told as fact is still a false report (Exo 23:1).

The real record is better. The 4th Brigade had already made its name near Verdun before Belleau Wood, and then held the wood at terrible cost. Truth needs no improving: whatsoever things are true, think on these things (Php 4:8).
roots_summary: Supposed German Teufelhunden (correctly Teufelshunde) → American newspapers, April 1918, crediting German troops → recruiting posters → Marine nickname. Belleau Wood origin contradicted by dates (USMC History Division, 2022).
roots_lines: March–May 1918: 4th Marine Brigade in the Toulon sector near Verdun
April 1918: American newspapers report German troops calling Marines Teufel Hunden (Boston Daily Globe, 14 April 1918, per NMMC)
June 1918: Belleau Wood, the battle later credited with the name in Marine tradition (USMC History Division, Marine Corps Lore, 1960)
2022: History Division journal Marine Corps History finds no evidence the Germans coined it
usage: “Every boot learns the devil dog story; a good NCO teaches him the dates too.”
A faithful witness will not lie: but a false witness will utter lies (Pro 14:5).

etymology: American sailors’ slang for a Marine, recorded by the National Museum of the Marine Corps as appearing as early as the Second World War. The museum’s explanation is that a Marine’s head rising out of the high collar of the dress blue coat looked like a Mason jar. Since the war the word has also been tied to the close-cropped “high and tight” haircut, and some Marines call that cut a “jarhead cut.” The museum gives no first written use for either. Merriam-Webster gives a first known use of 1934, earlier than the museum’s Second World War date.
biblical_def: Jarhead began as a jab and became a badge. The National Museum of the Marine Corps groups it with gyrene and grunt: words other servicemen meant as insults, which Marines took up with pride. The usual explanations are the high collar of the dress blues and the squared-off recruit haircut; Merriam-Webster dates it to 1934. The Christian observation: Scripture is not ashamed of plain vessels. “We have this treasure in earthen vessels, that the excellency of the power may be of God, and not of us” (2Co 4:7). A man mocked for his service has company: “Blessed are ye, when men shall revile you … for my sake” (Mat 5:11). Reviling for Christ is blessed; a nickname from the Navy is only ribbing.
webster_summary: Slang for a U.S. Marine, first known use 1934 (Merriam-Webster), sailors’ slang by the Second World War; usually said to come from the high dress-blue collar or the close haircut (NMMC). Exact origin disputed.
webster_full: JARHEAD, n. (Military slang) A U.S. Marine. First known use 1934 (Merriam-Webster); sailors’ slang by the Second World War (NMMC); usually explained by the high collar of the dress blue coat, from which the head rose like a Mason jar, and later by the close-cropped haircut (National Museum of the Marine Corps). Origin disputed.
scriptures: But we have this treasure in earthen vessels, that the excellency of the power may be of God, and not of us.
Blessed are ye, when men shall revile you, and persecute you, and shall say all manner of evil against you falsely, for my sake.
corruption_summary: A sailors’ jab turned into a Marine’s badge; harmless ribbing, so long as the ribbing never curdles into contempt.
corruption_paragraphs: Service rivalry is old and mostly good-natured. The danger comes when a nickname stops being banter between brothers and becomes contempt for men who serve.
Marines answered the jab by wearing it. That is a fair picture of the Christian answer to scorn: neither sulking nor striking back, but bearing the name with a good conscience (Mat 5:11).
roots_summary: jar + head → sailors’ slang for a Marine by the Second World War → usually explained by the dress-blue collar, later by the haircut (NMMC). Disputed.
roots_lines: 1934: first known use (Merriam-Webster)
Second World War: sailors call Marines jarheads (NMMC)
Explanation 1: head rising from the high dress-blue collar like a Mason jar
Explanation 2 (later): the close-cropped “high and tight” haircut, the “jarhead cut”
usage: “The chief called him a jarhead, and the corporal said, thank you, Chief.”
But we have this treasure in earthen vessels (2Co 4:7).

etymology: A Marine Corps cry of motivation and assent. A 2004 Marine Corps Training and Education Command article from Parris Island says it was not heard among Marines before 1950 and traces it to reconnaissance Marines of the 1st Amphibious Reconnaissance Company in 1953, who travelled by submarine: the dive klaxon sounded “Aarugha,” the recon Marines took up the sound during runs and physical training, and it wore down to “Oorah.” The article credits this account to a retired Marine major and cites a Marine Corps training reference on recon history titled “Aarugha”; it says drill instructors spread the word Corps-wide in the 1980s and 1990s. The account rests on one retired officer’s testimony and a training reference the article names but does not quote.
biblical_def: Oorah is young as Marine words go, and the Corps’ own account of it is careful: no Marine before 1950 is known to have said it, and its spread came through recon and then drill instructors. The best-supported story is the submarine klaxon heard by recon Marines in 1953. The Christian observation: a shout is not empty when it is joined to obedience. At Jericho the shout came at the word of the Lord and after six days of marching in silence: “all the people shall shout with a great shout; and the wall of the city shall fall down flat” (Jos 6:5). Zeal is good; zeal that obeys is better.
webster_summary: A Marine Corps cry of motivation; traced by a Marine Corps (TECOM) account to recon Marines aboard submarines in 1953, imitating the “Aarugha” dive klaxon. Origin disputed; popularized in the 1980s–1990s.
webster_full: OORAH, interj. (Marine Corps) A cry of motivation, greeting or assent. Traced by Marine Corps Training and Education Command (2004) to 1st Amphibious Reconnaissance Company Marines in 1953, who imitated a submarine dive klaxon (“Aarugha”); spread Corps-wide in the 1980s and 1990s. Origin disputed.
scriptures: And it shall come to pass, that when they make a long blast with the ram's horn, and when ye hear the sound of the trumpet, all the people shall shout with a great shout; and the wall of the city shall fall down flat, and the people shall ascend up every man straight before him.
Two are better than one; because they have a good reward for their labour.
corruption_summary: A shout of shared resolve; it goes hollow when it stands in for the work it is supposed to announce.
corruption_paragraphs: Any cry of motivation can be cheapened. Said a hundred times a day, it can become noise that covers for slack effort rather than a sign of real resolve.
Israel’s great shout at Jericho came after obedience, not instead of it (Jos 6:5). A cry is worth what the men behind it are willing to do.
roots_summary: Submarine dive klaxon “Aarugha” → 1st Amphibious Reconnaissance Company, 1953 → shortened to oorah → spread by drill instructors in the 1980s–1990s (TECOM, 2004). Disputed.
roots_lines: Before 1950: no record of Marines using the word (TECOM, 2004)
1953: recon Marines riding submarines take up the “Aarugha” dive klaxon as a cadence cry
1980s–1990s: drill instructors carry oorah through the whole Corps
usage: “The company answered the first sergeant with one loud oorah and stepped off.”
All the people shall shout with a great shout (Jos 6:5).

etymology: The scarlet stripe down the outer seam of the dress blue trousers worn by Marine officers, staff noncommissioned officers and noncommissioned officers. The USMC History Division’s Marine Corps Lore (1960) records the legend that it honours the blood shed at Chapultepec in 1847, and lists it among stories that are told rather than proved. The documented origin, per the National Museum of the Marine Corps, is uniform regulation: trouser stripes began in 1837, following the Army practice of matching the jacket facings, and were buff white at first; when the uniform returned to dark blue faced with red they became dark blue edged in red; they were made solid red in 1849; in 1859 regulations set a scarlet cord in the seam for NCOs and musicians and a scarlet welt for officers; the present plain scarlet stripe dates from 1904. The museum finds no evidence tying the stripe to Chapultepec.
biblical_def: The blood stripe is a real uniform item with a false origin story. The legend says it commemorates the Marines who fell storming Chapultepec in 1847. The record says trouser stripes were in the Marine uniform from 1837, ten years before the battle, and that their colour and cut changed by regulation several times, reaching today’s plain scarlet stripe in 1904. The Christian observation: honour the dead with the truth. “Buy the truth, and sell it not” (Pro 23:23). The Marines of 1847 were brave without a myth, and the true blood that purchased a people needs no embroidery: “without shedding of blood is no remission” (Heb 9:22).
webster_summary: The scarlet trouser stripe of Marine officers and NCOs; popularly said to honour Chapultepec (1847), but stripes were in the uniform from 1837 and reached their present form by regulation in 1904 (USMC History Division; NMMC). Folk myth.
webster_full: BLOOD STRIPE, n. (Marine Corps) The scarlet stripe on the outer seam of the dress blue trousers of officers, staff NCOs and NCOs. Popularly said to commemorate the Marines killed at Chapultepec in 1847; in fact trouser stripes date from 1837 and took their present plain scarlet form in 1904 (USMC History Division, Marine Corps Lore, 1960; National Museum of the Marine Corps).
scriptures: Buy the truth, and sell it not; also wisdom, and instruction, and understanding.
And almost all things are by the law purged with blood; and without shedding of blood is no remission.
Greater love hath no man than this, that a man lay down his life for his friends.
corruption_summary: A real uniform item dressed in a false story; the Marines of Chapultepec deserve the true record, not a legend.
corruption_paragraphs: The Chapultepec story is told with love, and it is false in its facts. Repeating it does the fallen no honour; it puts a fable where the record should stand (Pro 23:23).
The stripe can still mean what the Corps says it means: that leading Marines may cost a man his life (Joh 15:13). That meaning does not depend on the legend, and it is better for being true.
roots_summary: Trouser stripes, 1837 (buff white) → dark blue edged red → solid red, 1849 → scarlet cord / welt, 1859 → plain scarlet stripe, 1904 (NMMC). Chapultepec legend recorded by USMC History Division (1960). Folk myth.
roots_lines: 1837: trouser stripes introduced, buff white, after Army practice (NMMC)
1847: Chapultepec, the battle the legend later attached to the stripe
1849: stripes made solid red
1859: scarlet cord for NCOs and musicians, scarlet welt for officers
1904: the present plain scarlet stripe adopted
usage: “He earned his blood stripe as a corporal and wore it to his grandson’s wedding.”
Greater love hath no man than this, that a man lay down his life for his friends (Joh 15:13).

etymology: A British naval saying, older than its famous story. The fuller form appears in John Davis’s novel The Post-Captain (1804): “He may tell that to the marines, but the sailors will not believe him.” The marines meant were British marines, held by sailors to be green and easy to fool (Phrase Finder). Phrase Finder’s earliest short form is 1846. The popular tale that King Charles II coined the phrase in 1664 after a Marine colonel vouched for flying fish is told by the Marine Corps History Division as a legend (Marine Corps Lore, 1960). Phrase Finder reports that the tale was shown to be a hoax written in the 1900s by the novelist W. P. Drury, a retired Royal Marine officer.
biblical_def: Tell it to the Marines is a scornful answer to a story nobody believes. Sailors said it first, about the soldiers who served aboard their ships. The fuller form ran, "He may tell that to the marines, but the sailors will not believe him" (1804). The best-known story of its origin is a fable. In that story King Charles II doubts a sea captain’s report of fish that fly, a Marine colonel vouches for it, and the king rules that any unlikely yarn should be told to the Marines. The History Division prints the story as a legend. Phrase Finder reports it was written up in the 1900s as a hoax. So the phrase about believing tall tales came wrapped in a tall tale of its own. Scripture is not impressed by a good yarn: "The simple believeth every word: but the prudent man looketh well to his going" (Pro 14:15). The apostles staked the Gospel on the opposite of a fable: "we have not followed cunningly devised fables ... but were eyewitnesses of his majesty" (2Pe 1:16). The rule for every Marine and every Christian is the same: "Prove all things; hold fast that which is good" (1Th 5:21).
webster_summary: A scornful reply to an unbelievable story; British naval in origin, on record by 1804. The tale that Charles II coined it is a later hoax. Prove all things (1Th 5:21); the Gospel is no cunningly devised fable (2Pe 1:16).
webster_full: TELL IT TO THE MARINES, phr. An expression of disbelief; short for “tell that to the marines, but the sailors will not believe it.” British naval slang; the long form is in John Davis, The Post-Captain (1804) (Phrase Finder).

Myth note: the story of Charles II, Samuel Pepys and the flying fish is printed by the USMC History Division as a legend, and is reported by Phrase Finder to be a hoax from the 1900s by W. P. Drury. The documented origin is the older sailors’ saying.
scriptures: The simple believeth every word: but the prudent man looketh well to his going.
Prove all things; hold fast that which is good.
For we have not followed cunningly devised fables, when we made known unto you the power and coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, but were eyewitnesses of his majesty.
But refuse profane and old wives' fables, and exercise thyself rather unto godliness.
He that is first in his own cause seemeth just; but his neighbour cometh and searcheth him.
corruption_summary: The saying mocks the easily fooled, but its most famous origin story fooled almost everyone; the cure is to test the story before you repeat it.
corruption_paragraphs: Barracks lore, internet lists and pulpit illustrations all pass along stories that sound right and were never checked. The flying-fish tale ran for most of a century before anyone traced it. "He that is first in his own cause seemeth just; but his neighbour cometh and searcheth him" (Pro 18:17).
The Christian is commanded to refuse "profane and old wives’ fables" (1Ti 4:7). That includes the pleasant ones about our own heritage. Truth honors the Corps better than legend does.
roots_summary: British sailors’ scorn for shipboard marines → “tell that to the marines, but the sailors will not believe him” (1804) → short form (Phrase Finder’s earliest, 1846) → a 1900s hoax story about Charles II.
roots_lines: 1804: long form in John Davis, The Post-Captain (Phrase Finder)
1846: short form “tell it to the marines” in a printed preface (Phrase Finder)
1900s: the Charles II and flying-fish story, reported as a hoax by W. P. Drury (Phrase Finder)
1960: USMC History Division prints the Charles II story under “Marine Corps Legends”
usage: "He says the recruiter promised him a beach house. Tell it to the Marines."
The simple believeth every word: but the prudent man looketh well to his going. (Pro 14:15).
Prove all things; hold fast that which is good. (1Th 5:21).

etymology: Latin semper (always) + fidelis (faithful), from fides, faith. The USMC History Division records that Semper Fidelis was adopted as the motto of the Corps about 1883, when, the National Museum of the Marine Corps notes, Colonel Charles G. McCawley was Commandant. Before that there were three traditional, unofficial mottoes: Fortitudine (“with fortitude”), from before the War of 1812; “By Sea and by Land,” a translation of the Royal Marines’ Per Mare, Per Terram; and “To the Shores of Tripoli,” revised in 1848 to “From the Halls of the Montezumas to the Shores of Tripoli.” The Corps shares the motto with Britain’s Devonshire Regiment (the 11th Foot). The museum notes the reasons for the choice are unclear.
biblical_def: Semper Fidelis is Latin for “always faithful” — since about 1883 the motto of the United States Marine Corps. Scripture commends the same disposition continually: be thou faithful unto death, and I will give thee a crown of life. The Marine's semper fi and the saint's perseverance share a vocabulary; for the Christian Marine, they share an object.
webster_summary: (Latin.) Always faithful; the motto of the U.S. Marine Corps; by extension, the disposition of unbroken loyalty.
webster_full: Adopted as the Marine Corps motto in 1883, replacing earlier mottos. The Latin is brief and uncompromising: at all times, in all circumstances, faithful.
Scripture's parallel commendation in Revelation 2:10 is the saint's version: be thou faithful unto death. The crown of life follows, not as wage but as gift to the faithful.
scriptures: Be thou faithful unto death, and I will give thee a crown of life.
Moreover it is required in stewards, that a man be found faithful.
Well done, thou good and faithful servant: thou hast been faithful over a few things, I will make thee ruler over many things.
corruption_summary: Modern culture rotates loyalties as conditions change; the Marine's semper fi and the saint's perseverance both witness against the rotation.
corruption_paragraphs: Faithfulness is a hard discipline because conditions change and the unfaithful keep moving. Semper is the difficult word: always. Not when convenient, not when reciprocated, not when noticed.

Scripture commends the same standard. The crown of life is for the saint who is faithful unto death, not unto comfort. The Marine and the saint share a discipline; for the Christian Marine, they share an Object.
roots_summary: Latin compound semper fidelis; U.S. Marine Corps motto from about 1883 (USMC History Division), after Fortitudine, “By Sea and by Land” and “To the Shores of Tripoli”; biblical equivalent in Hebrew emunah and Greek pistis / pistos.
roots_lines: Latin semper (always) plus fidelis (faithful) — from fides, faith, faithfulness.
Hebrew emunah — faithfulness, steadfastness; behind ‘great is thy faithfulness’ (Lam 3:23).

About 1883: adopted as the Marine Corps motto; earlier traditional mottoes Fortitudine, “By Sea and by Land,” “To the Shores of Tripoli” (USMC History Division). Col. Charles G. McCawley was then Commandant (NMMC)
usage: Semper Fidelis is the discipline that does not rotate.
Be thou faithful unto death — the saint's version.
For the Christian Marine, semper fi and the gospel share an Object.
